content: 1. Treatment support provided by trained lay providers or healthcare workers is recommended over treatment support administered by family members or unsupported treatment. This recommendation is conditional and based on very low certainty in the evidence. 2. Video-supported treatment (VST) can replace traditional treatment support when video communication technology is available and can be appropriately organized and operated by healthcare providers and patients. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty in the evidence. 3. Patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) should primarily receive ambulatory care rather than care models based on hospitalization. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty in the evidence. 4. A decentralized model of care is recommended over a centralized model for patients undergoing MDR-TB treatment. This recommendation is conditional and based on very low certainty in the evidence. 5. Tracers, such as SMS, telephone calls, or home visits, are used to maintain communication with patients. 6. Digital medication monitors are devices that record the time between openings of a pillbox. These monitors may include audio reminders or send SMS notifications to remind patients to take their medications. 7. Material support for patients can include food or financial assistance, such as meals, food baskets, food supplements, food vouchers, transport subsidies, living allowances, housing incentives, or financial bonuses. This support aims to address indirect costs incurred by patients or their caregivers in accessing healthcare services and mitigate income loss due to the disease. 8. Psychological support may involve counseling sessions or peer-group support. 9. Staff education can include adherence education, visual reminders, educational tools, and decision-making aids. 10. Routine HIV testing should be offered to all patients with presumptive or diagnosed tuberculosis. This is a strong recommendation with low certainty in the evidence. 11. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for infants, children, and adolescents living with HIV, regardless of clinical or immune conditions. Priority should be given to children under five years old and those with severe or advanced HIV disease. This is a strong recommendation with high certainty in the evidence. 12. In settings with high prevalence of malaria or severe bacterial infections, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should continue into adulthood, regardless of whether antiretroviral therapy (ART) is provided. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate certainty in the evidence. 13. In low-prevalence settings for malaria and bacterial infections, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis may be discontinued for children aged five years and older who are clinically stable and virally suppressed on ART for at least six months, with a CD4 count >350 cells/mm³. This is a strong recommendation with very low certainty in the evidence. 14. ART should be initiated for all people living with HIV, regardless of WHO clinical stage or CD4 cell count. This includes pregnant and breastfeeding women, adolescents, children aged one to less than ten years, and infants diagnosed in the first year of life. Rapid ART initiation should be offered within seven days of HIV diagnosis, with same-day initiation for those ready to start. This is a strong recommendation with high certainty in the evidence for adults and adolescents, but low certainty for children. 15. ART should be started as soon as possible within two weeks of initiating TB treatment for adolescents and children living with HIV, except in cases of meningitis. This is a strong recommendation with varying levels of evidence certainty. 16. For TB meningitis, ART initiation should be delayed by at least four weeks and started within eight weeks of TB treatment initiation. 17. Dolutegravir (DTG) combined with a nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) backbone is the preferred first-line ART regimen for people living with HIV. This is strongly recommended for adolescents and conditionally recommended for children with approved DTG dosing. 18. For neonates, a raltegravir (RAL)-based regimen may be recommended as the preferred first-line ART regimen. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty in the evidence. 19. DTG with an optimized NRTI backbone may be recommended as a preferred second-line ART regimen for individuals failing non-DTG-based regimens. This is conditionally recommended for adolescents and children with approved DTG dosing. 20. Boosted protease inhibitors with an optimized NRTI backbone are recommended as a preferred second-line ART regimen for individuals failing DTG-based regimens. This is a strong recommendation with moderate certainty in the evidence. 21. Infants with severe acute malnutrition admitted for inpatient care should receive parenteral antibiotics to treat possible sepsis and appropriate treatment for other medical complications, such as tuberculosis, HIV, surgical conditions, or disability. This is a strong recommendation with very low certainty in the evidence. 22. School-age children, adolescents, and adults with TB disease and severe acute malnutrition should be treated according to WHO recommendations for managing severe acute malnutrition. This is a strong recommendation with very low certainty in the evidence. 23. Children under five years old with TB disease and severe acute malnutrition should be managed according to WHO guidelines for severe acute malnutrition in children under five. This is a strong recommendation with very low certainty in the evidence. 24. School-age children, adolescents, and adults with TB disease and moderate undernutrition who fail to regain normal BMI after two months of TB treatment, or who lose weight during treatment, should be evaluated for adherence and comorbid conditions. They should receive nutritional assessment, counseling, and locally available nutrient-rich or fortified supplementary foods as needed. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty in the evidence. 25. Children under five years old with TB disease and moderate undernutrition should be managed like other children with moderate undernutrition, including provision of locally available nutrient-rich or fortified supplementary foods to restore appropriate weight-for-height. This is a strong recommendation with very low certainty in the evidence. 26. Patients with MDR-TB and moderate undernutrition should receive locally available nutrient-rich or fortified supplementary foods as necessary to restore normal nutritional status. This is a strong recommendation with very low certainty in the evidence. 27. A daily multiple micronutrient supplement at 1× recommended nutrient intake should be provided in situations where fortified or supplementary foods are unavailable. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty in the evidence. 28. Household contacts of TB patients should undergo nutritional screening and assessment as part of contact investigation. If malnutrition is identified, it should be managed according to WHO recommendations. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty in the evidence. 29. Pyridoxine supplementation is recommended alongside isoniazid treatment for all pregnant or breastfeeding women, as well as individuals with conditions such as HIV infection, alcohol dependency, malnutrition, diabetes, chronic liver disease, or renal failure. 30. Research priorities include evaluating the use of molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostics for screening children and adolescents, developing better screening tools and approaches for specific age groups, determining optimal screening frequency for high-risk subpopulations, and conducting clinical trials to assess patient-important outcomes for TB screening in children. 31. Diagnostic approaches should include external validation of newly developed integrated treatment decision algorithms, operational research on their use and impact, and modeling studies to determine their potential effect on case detection and treatment initiation.
